contextual_paragraphs.html: We present a comparative analysis of text complexity across domains using scale-free metrics. We quantify linguistic complexity via Heaps’ exponent β\beta (vocabulary growth), Taylor’s exponent α\alpha (word-frequency fluctuation scaling), compression rate rr (redundancy), and entropy. Our corpora span three domains: legal documents (statutes, cases, deeds) as a specialized domain, general natural language texts (literature, Wikipedia), and AI-generated (GPT) text. We find that legal texts exhibit slower vocabulary growth (lower β\beta) and higher term consistency (higher α\alpha) than general texts. Within legal domain, statutory codes have the lowest β\beta and highest α\alpha, reflecting strict drafting conventions, while cases and deeds show higher β\beta and lower α\alpha. In contrast, GPT-generated text shows the statistics more aligning with general language patterns. These results demonstrate that legal texts exhibit domain-specific structures and complexities, which current generative models do not fully replicate.

In this work, we consider how such characteristics of legal text can be quantified by complexity measures. Our analysis reveals that legal texts exhibit distinctive statistical patterns: specifically, they have slower vocabulary growth (smaller β\beta) and greater term consistency (larger α\alpha) than general-language texts. In contrast, GPT-generated texts show higher β\beta and lower α\alpha, aligning more closely with general language patterns.

Regarding the frequency distribution, Zipf’s law is the best-known power-law property of language, describing the relationship between word frequency rank and frequency. However, because the Zipf exponent is close to −1-1 for most natural texts, Zipf’s law alone does not distinguish between corpora. We therefore focus on the type-token relationship (Heaps’ law). Excluding token types with zero variance, we perform a linear regression and take the slope α\alpha as the Taylor exponent [31]. Taylor’s exponent α\alpha is 0.5 for a shuffled text, and 0.5<α<10.5<\alpha<1 for natural texts [25]. We compute α\alpha in order to capture contextual clustering of words: a higher α\alpha indicates a greater context dependence.

We will reserve discussion of this measure till Sec. 6.4, where we show that, by itself, HnormH_{\mathrm{norm}} does not effectively distinguish text types. In the following sections, our primary analysis focuses on the scale‐free exponents β\beta, α\alpha (Sect. 3.1) and the compression rate rr.

In the following subsections, we concentrate on the three primary scale‐free measures: Heaps’ exponent β\beta, Taylor’s exponent α\alpha, and gzip compression rate rr. All of the resulting values are shown in Table  2. The normalized vocabulary entropy HnormH_{\mathrm{norm}} will be revisited in Section 6.4, where we demonstrate that, alone, it does not reliably distinguish text types.

Figure 2 plots Taylor’s exponent α\alpha against Heaps’ exponent β\beta for each category, while Figure 3 shows the distribution of compression rates rr. Together, these measures trace a coherent signature of text complexity.

The results of (β,α,r)(\beta,\alpha,r) reveal that legal drafting conventions impose a distinct complex structure—slow β\beta, high α\alpha, high rr—which general‐purpose and AI‐generated texts do not naturally replicate.

Figure 4 shows α\alpha vs. β\beta for statutes, cases, and deeds, with compression rates reported in Table 2 (3rd column). Statutes (French Code, U.S. Code, Australian corpus) cluster at low β\beta (0.521 - 0.674), high α\alpha (0.655 – 0.711), and the highest rr (4.56 – 4.68), reflecting uniform, precise drafting. Case opinions (Harvard Case Law: β=0.622\beta=0.622, α=0.647\alpha=0.647, r=3.28r=3.28) sit slightly lower and on the right, indicating greater lexical flexibility balanced by moderate redundancy.

Figure 5 compares legal corpora (green) with ChatGPT outputs (gray) in the α\alpha–β\beta plane (the compression rates are in Table 2). GPT‐generated texts shift toward higher β\beta and lower α\alpha, reflecting faster vocabulary turnover and weaker clustering. Moreover, their tight clustering (occupying a small, compact region) signals a lack of variance in generative behavior. Lower rr values further underscore reduced redundancy compared to human‐authored legal drafts.

By contrast, the compression rate rr proves to be a more effective single-axis metric, a conclusion which is consistent with a number of previous studies [26, 27]. As shown in Fig. 6(b) and Fig. 3, literature and Wikipedia samples occupy the lowest rr values, legal texts occupy the highest, and case opinions and GPT-generated outputs fall in between. Notably, some ChatGPT-generated case-law samples achieve compression rates nearly on par with human-authored statutes, indicating that rr can sometimes overlap across genres—but crucially it still orders the majority of categories in a coherent hierarchy of redundancy.

Despite rr’s discriminative power, our scatterplot of Taylor’s α\alpha versus Heaps’ β\beta (Fig. 2) reveals an even richer separation. GPT-generated texts form a tight, low-variance cluster in the (β,α)(\beta,\alpha) plane, as discussed in Sec. 6.1, clearly distinct from both literature and legal corpora. This compact clustering highlights GPT’s limited diversity in vocabulary growth and term consistency, whereas combining β\beta, α\alpha, and rr provides a multidimensional signature that robustly captures domain-specific drafting conventions—something normalized entropy alone cannot achieve.

Our investigation shows that legal language, shaped by precise and repetitive drafting conventions, differs fundamentally from general natural language: it introduces new vocabulary more slowly (lower Heaps’ exponent β\beta), enforces greater term consistency (higher Taylor’s exponent α\alpha), and exhibits higher redundancy (rr) to minimize ambiguity. GPT-generated texts, by contrast, cluster tightly, display more rapid vocabulary growth, and yield reduced redundancy, highlighting that current language models, while proficient in general prose, struggle to replicate true legal writing and lack sufficient variance.

Prior work has shown exceptionally high Taylor’s α\alpha in programming-language corpora [16], suggesting that domain-specific discourse structures drive these complexity signatures. Future efforts should explore fine‐tuning language models to respect such scale‐free patterns—across legal, code, and other specialized genres—to enable AI systems that truly understand and generate text with the appropriate statistical and logical conventions.

With the advent of AI, legal texts have become an important challenge in the fields of AI and NLP. Legal texts exhibit probabilistic patterns as in the natural language [24, 9], but there is more. Above all, legal texts are considered difficult because they employ specialized vocabulary and follow rigorous drafting conventions [3, 15], and legal discourse must be consistent in its content to adjudicate human behavior [17, 10].

In this work, we consider how such characteristics of legal text can be quantified by complexity measures. Our analysis reveals that legal texts exhibit distinctive statistical patterns: specifically, they have slower vocabulary growth (smaller β\beta) and greater term consistency (larger α\alpha) than general-language texts. In contrast, GPT-generated texts show higher β\beta and lower α\alpha, aligning more closely with general language patterns.

The perspective of this study differs from previous substantial works on categorization and clustering, which use supervised or unsupervised methods that use classification accuracy to distinguish legal from general text, but lack an explicit mathematical rationale for the underlying differences. Instead, we show that the key divergence between legal and general texts lies in their scale-free discourse structure.

Understanding these complexity signatures is crucial for processing legal texts, as the current AIs themselves exhibit scale-free behavior [14], but we show that they are limited in their capability of capturing legal drafting conventions. We argue that our findings must motivate a fundamental reconsideration of processing strategies and provide a road map for analyzing other challenging text genres.

Efforts to adapt AI to legal language include domain-specific pre-training (e.g., Legal-BERT [6] on statutes, opinions, and contracts) and generic models on benchmarks such as LexGLUE [8]. Extensions of neural network architectures, such as Longformer, can tackle ultra-long documents, while multi-label classification further refines performance [1, 5]. However, these methods primarily measure success through accuracy in downstream tasks and treat legal texts as classification targets rather than analyzing their linguistic complexity. By contrast, our approach explicitly quantifies textual characteristics— vocabulary growth, contextual clustering, and redundancy—thereby uncovering statistical signatures inherent in legal language that conventional AI approaches typically overlook.

With the advent of AI, legal texts have become an important challenge in the fields of AI and NLP. Legal texts exhibit probabilistic patterns as in the natural language [24, 9], but there is more. Above all, legal texts are considered difficult because they employ specialized vocabulary and follow rigorous drafting conventions [3, 15], and legal discourse must be consistent in its content to adjudicate human behavior [17, 10].

In this work, we consider how such characteristics of legal text can be quantified by complexity measures. Our analysis reveals that legal texts exhibit distinctive statistical patterns: specifically, they have slower vocabulary growth (smaller β\beta) and greater term consistency (larger α\alpha) than general-language texts. In contrast, GPT-generated texts show higher β\beta and lower α\alpha, aligning more closely with general language patterns.

The perspective of this study differs from previous substantial works on categorization and clustering, which use supervised or unsupervised methods that use classification accuracy to distinguish legal from general text, but lack an explicit mathematical rationale for the underlying differences. Instead, we show that the key divergence between legal and general texts lies in their scale-free discourse structure.

Understanding these complexity signatures is crucial for processing legal texts, as the current AIs themselves exhibit scale-free behavior [14], but we show that they are limited in their capability of capturing legal drafting conventions. We argue that our findings must motivate a fundamental reconsideration of processing strategies and provide a road map for analyzing other challenging text genres.

The exponent β\beta is 1 for certain random texts, but for natural language it is typically smaller (often around 0.7) [29]. Later, we will show that specialized domain texts tend to have even smaller β\beta values, indicating slower vocabulary growth.

Similarly, Fig. 1(b) and Fig. 1(d) show Taylor’s analysis: the literature example has a smaller α\alpha, whereas the U.S. Code example’s larger α\alpha indicates more clustered word usage. We also computed the compression rate for these two examples: U.S. Code (r=4.383r=4.383) versus literature (r=2.577r=2.577). The higher compression for the Code reflects its greater repetitiveness. In the following sections, we show that these tendencies generalize across our datasets.

Legal texts: Statutory law (French Code, U.S. Code, Australian legislation [4]), cases (the Caselaw Access Project [22]), and contract provisions (patents, the LED-GAR corpus of contract clauses [33], and a German contracts corpus [19]).

In the following subsections, we concentrate on the three primary scale‐free measures: Heaps’ exponent β\beta, Taylor’s exponent α\alpha, and gzip compression rate rr. All of the resulting values are shown in Table  2. The normalized vocabulary entropy HnormH_{\mathrm{norm}} will be revisited in Section 6.4, where we demonstrate that, alone, it does not reliably distinguish text types.

Legal corpora (green) occupy the upper‐left region of the α\alpha–β\beta plane, combining slow vocabulary growth (β=0.521​–​0.674\beta=0.521–0.674) with strong term clustering (α=0.624​–​0.733\alpha=0.624–0.733), and elevated redundancy (r=3.281​–​4.684r=3.281–4.684). In contrast, literature (orange) lies toward the lower‐right, with higher β=0.623\beta=0.623, lower α=0.576\alpha=0.576, and reduced redundancy (r=2.634r=2.634).

GPT‐generated texts (gray) mirror general‐language patterns in both scale-free metrics: β≈0.65\beta\approx 0.65 and α≈0.60\alpha\approx 0.60. Notably, ChatGPT points cluster tightly in a compact region of the α\alpha–β\beta plane, indicating limited variance in term‐introduction and clustering behaviors. Their compression rates overlap with legal texts, as shown in Fig. 3, suggesting that rr alone may not suffice for clear separation between AI-generated and human-written texts, which will also be discussed in Sec.6 .

The results of (β,α,r)(\beta,\alpha,r) reveal that legal drafting conventions impose a distinct complex structure—slow β\beta, high α\alpha, high rr—which general‐purpose and AI‐generated texts do not naturally replicate.

Figure 5 compares legal corpora (green) with ChatGPT outputs (gray) in the α\alpha–β\beta plane (the compression rates are in Table 2). GPT‐generated texts shift toward higher β\beta and lower α\alpha, reflecting faster vocabulary turnover and weaker clustering. Moreover, their tight clustering (occupying a small, compact region) signals a lack of variance in generative behavior. Lower rr values further underscore reduced redundancy compared to human‐authored legal drafts.

One previous work [12] employs a two‐dimensional plot of normalized vocabulary entropy HnormH_{\mathrm{norm}} (See Sec. 3.2) against gzip compression rate rr, suggesting that legal and general‐language texts occupy distinct regions in redundancy space. Crucially, this figure confines HnormH_{\mathrm{norm}} (vertical axis) to a narrow interval 0.72–0.82, which visually amplifies small corpus‐to‐corpus differences. When we tried to replot our data points (Fig. 6(b)), these apparent separations vanished, revealing a single, continuous trend rather than discrete clusters. In other words, HnormH_{\mathrm{norm}} does not distinguish different kinds of texts by itself.

By contrast, the compression rate rr proves to be a more effective single-axis metric, a conclusion which is consistent with a number of previous studies [26, 27]. As shown in Fig. 6(b) and Fig. 3, literature and Wikipedia samples occupy the lowest rr values, legal texts occupy the highest, and case opinions and GPT-generated outputs fall in between. Notably, some ChatGPT-generated case-law samples achieve compression rates nearly on par with human-authored statutes, indicating that rr can sometimes overlap across genres—but crucially it still orders the majority of categories in a coherent hierarchy of redundancy.

Despite rr’s discriminative power, our scatterplot of Taylor’s α\alpha versus Heaps’ β\beta (Fig. 2) reveals an even richer separation. GPT-generated texts form a tight, low-variance cluster in the (β,α)(\beta,\alpha) plane, as discussed in Sec. 6.1, clearly distinct from both literature and legal corpora. This compact clustering highlights GPT’s limited diversity in vocabulary growth and term consistency, whereas combining β\beta, α\alpha, and rr provides a multidimensional signature that robustly captures domain-specific drafting conventions—something normalized entropy alone cannot achieve.

Our investigation shows that legal language, shaped by precise and repetitive drafting conventions, differs fundamentally from general natural language: it introduces new vocabulary more slowly (lower Heaps’ exponent β\beta), enforces greater term consistency (higher Taylor’s exponent α\alpha), and exhibits higher redundancy (rr) to minimize ambiguity. GPT-generated texts, by contrast, cluster tightly, display more rapid vocabulary growth, and yield reduced redundancy, highlighting that current language models, while proficient in general prose, struggle to replicate true legal writing and lack sufficient variance.

Prior work has shown exceptionally high Taylor’s α\alpha in programming-language corpora [16], suggesting that domain-specific discourse structures drive these complexity signatures. Future efforts should explore fine‐tuning language models to respect such scale‐free patterns—across legal, code, and other specialized genres—to enable AI systems that truly understand and generate text with the appropriate statistical and logical conventions.

contextual_paragraphs.html: We present a comparative analysis of text complexity across domains using scale-free metrics. We quantify linguistic complexity via Heaps’ exponent β\beta (vocabulary growth), Taylor’s exponent α\alpha (word-frequency fluctuation scaling), compression rate rr (redundancy), and entropy. Our corpora span three domains: legal documents (statutes, cases, deeds) as a specialized domain, general natural language texts (literature, Wikipedia), and AI-generated (GPT) text. We find that legal texts exhibit slower vocabulary growth (lower β\beta) and higher term consistency (higher α\alpha) than general texts. Within legal domain, statutory codes have the lowest β\beta and highest α\alpha, reflecting strict drafting conventions, while cases and deeds show higher β\beta and lower α\alpha. In contrast, GPT-generated text shows the statistics more aligning with general language patterns. These results demonstrate that legal texts exhibit domain-specific structures and complexities, which current generative models do not fully replicate.

On the basis of scale-free metrics, we consider the gzip-based compression rate rr. Previous studies have shown that rr follows a power law scaling with text size (e.g., [29]) and that legal drafting yields higher rr than literary prose [12]. In this study, we include this compression rate and provide evidence of both its effectiveness and its limitations.

This section describes the methodology used to assess the differences in complexity between the text categories. We propose two types of metrics: scale-free properties (our original focus) and general metrics (compression rate), which have frequently been used in previous work on text complexity [15, 26, 12].

Texts often exhibit universal statistical behaviors in the form of scale-free properties, meaning these properties hold regardless of text size. This scale-free quality is crucial because many statistical metrics, including entropy, typically depend on the corpus size [30]. A comprehensive summary of scale-free properties is given in [29], which categorizes them into frequency distribution and long-memory aspects. We will demonstrate that different text domains possess distinct characteristics in both of these aspects.

Information‐theoretic measures have long been used to investigate legal language complexity. Early work used Shannon entropy [24] to distinguish legal from general‐language corpora [15]. [12] later proposed pairing a “normalized vocabulary entropy” with a gzip‐based compression rate to separate text types.
